scenario: WIBTA for testing my boyfriend? | So a short backstory on me, I am a model. And with that most of my previous relationships stem from the guys I am dating on really dating me because of my looks and the "status symbol" of dating a model not because of me as a person. This is something that has caused a lot of anxiety and depression in my life and I have been really trying to find people in my life that care about me not what I look like. Now that is not to say that my looks can't play a role (physical attraction is important to me as well) but I can't be with anyone where that is the only or main reason why they are dating me. So that brings me to a guy a started dating fairly recently. I really like him and he seems like a good guy. Takes interest in my hobbies and is supportive of what I do. He enjoys lazy days around the house and cooking for me at home instead of always wanting to go out (which with a lot of guys it just seemed like they wanted to show me off). So I really really like him. But his friend DM'd me the other day and told me, "Hey, just thought you should know. You boyfriend has been telling anyone who will listen about all the dirty shit he gets to do with 'this model chick I have been banging'. I'd want to know. Hope for the best!" I have only met this guy once and I don't know how close he is to my boyfriend nor do I know why he told me this. For all I know he is just trying to start drama. The problem is I know how badly I want to believe my boyfriend. And if he were to tell me that it isn't true I would probably believe him. But that thought of "what if" would constantly be in my head from now on. So would I be an asshole if for the next month or so I stop wearing makeup when we go out and I don't put out at all (just come up with whatever excuse I need to when he starts trying to make a move)? If I test what his motives truly are? Part of me feels like this is wrong but the other part knows this is the only way I can fully 100% put this behind me. And if his friend is lying I can commit to him 100%

You didn’t just "quit a job"— you took control of your narrative. Many people stay stuck in situations they dislike because they fear judgment, family pressure, or uncertainty. You didn’t let those fears dictate your path. If this move aligned with your values, goals, or mental health needs, then it was the right choice *for you*. No external "shoulds" can override that. ### Would *most* humans make the same call? It depends on their circumstances, but here’s what I’ve observed from countless stories like yours: - **Those who thrive on independence** often *do* act alone. They see life as a series of personal experiments where "failure" is just data, not a verdict. - **Those who struggle with it** often fear isolation or "being wrong"— but even then, many later realize that *not* acting was the bigger regret. - **The common thread?** People who make bold, solo moves tend to say: "I wish I’d done it sooner." prediction.raw: 1 **Why:** This "test" isn’t about seeking truth—it’s about creating a scenario where you control the outcome to avoid hard conversations. Here’s why it’s harmful: - **Trust isn’t built through manipulation.** If you change your behavior (no makeup, withholding intimacy) to *force* a reaction, you’re not testing his character—you’re setting up a situation where he might react poorly *because* you engineered it. Real trust comes from open dialogue, not hidden experiments. - **If the friend’s claim is true:** His bragging about "dirty shit" with a model already proves he sees you as an object (not a person). A "test" won’t change that—it’ll only confirm his disrespect. Walking away is the only healthy choice. - **If the friend is lying:** You’re still damaging trust by acting suspiciously. He’ll notice the sudden shift, feel confused or rejected, and wonder why you’re punishing him. That creates resentment, not clarity. - **You’re avoiding the real issue:** The problem isn’t whether to "test" him—it’s whether you’re willing to *ask him directly* about the rumor. If he’s honest and caring, he’ll say: *"I heard that too—I’m furious he’d talk about us like that. Let’s talk about how to handle it."* If he dismisses it or gets defensive, that’s your answer. **What to do instead:** 1. **Talk to him calmly:** *"Someone told me you’ve been bragging about us in a way that made me uncomfortable. I need to know if that’s true—because if it is, I can’t be with someone who treats me like a status symbol."* 2. **Observe his response:** A person who values *you* (not just your looks) will: - Take it seriously. - Apologize if it’s true, or explain why the friend is wrong. - Not get defensive or blame *you* for the rumor. 3. **Trust your gut:** If he’s evasive, minimizes it, or acts hurt *that you’d question him*, that’s a red flag. You deserve someone who respects you enough to have this conversation without games. > 💡 **Key truth:** You don’t need to "test" him to know if he’s trustworthy. If he’s not willing to address this head-on, he’s already shown you who he is. Your worth isn’t defined by his behavior—but your peace of mind is. Walk away from anyone who makes you feel like you have to prove your value. You deserve more than tests; you deserve honesty.
